title: Limits of monetary policy
log: 2026-10-29T12:22:33Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: The bank's monetary policy point covers how rate changes and QE move aggregate demand, not the limits of monetary policy such as time lags, its inability to target one region or industry, and global shocks, so this is a new point.

draft.title: Limits of monetary policy
card: A change in the cash rate takes time to affect spending and inflation. The delay is long and uneven, so the effect can arrive later than the RBA expects.
One cash rate applies to the whole economy. Monetary policy cannot target one region or industry, so it cannot cool a booming city and help a struggling town at the same time.
Events overseas, such as a world recession or a fall in export prices, can weaken the effect of a rate change. The RBA does not control them.
These limits mean monetary policy may not fully achieve its goals, so governments also use other policies.
draft.remember: Monetary policy can be slow, blunt and knocked off course by events overseas.

a.q: Why can monetary policy not fix a slump in one industry while the rest of the economy grows strongly?
opts: One cash rate applies across the whole economy
The cash rate only affects the dollar and not borrowing
The effects of a rate change arrive within a few days
The RBA cannot change the cash rate in a slump
a.why: The cash rate is a single rate for the whole economy, so it cannot be aimed at one industry. Time lags are a different limit: they affect when the policy works, not where it works.
a.clue: Think about how many cash rates there are.

b.q: The RBA cuts the cash rate to lift spending. Soon after, a sharp fall in world demand cuts Australian export earnings, and spending stays weak. Which limit does this best show?
opts: Global events can weaken the effect of policy
Time lags make the effect arrive later than expected
Policy cannot target one region or industry
The RBA has no control over the cash rate
b.why: The weak spending comes from a fall in world demand, which is a global event the RBA does not control. A time lag would be a delay in the effect of the rate cut, but the scenario points to an outside shock working against it.
b.clue: Look for where the cause of the weak spending comes from.

a.best: One cash rate applies across the whole economy

b.best: Global events can weaken the effect of policy
